title: Sonali Bendre Walked Back Onto Screen After Cancer and Delivered the Performance of Her Life. Raakh Is the Reason to Subscribe This Month.
excerpt: Prime Video's eight-episode crime drama reopens the 1978 Ranga-Billa wound — and Karan Johar says he 'may not recover soon.' Streaming now in 240 countries.
body:
The screen goes dark, and it stays dark long after the eighth episode ends. That is the trick **Raakh** pulls — a crime thriller that arrives dressed as a horror film and refuses to give you the clean snap of handcuffs you came for. By the time the credits roll, your brain is numb and there is no sigh of relief. That is the point.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=RdB_TgwLPqs</youtube>

Prime Video dropped all eight episodes on June 12, and within days the Indian film industry was talking about one thing: the return of **Sonali Bendre**. The actress, who stepped away from screens during her very public battle with metastatic cancer, comes back not as a glamorous comeback vehicle but as Mona Arora — a mother hollowed out by the disappearance of her two children. It is raw, unvarnished, devastating work, and it is being called the finest of her career.

She is not alone in earning that praise. **Karan Johar**, never one to undersell a reaction, posted that the show left him unable to sleep.

> "What I can't get out of my head are the career defining performances of Sonali Bendre and Aamir Bashir. Their portrayal of the pained parents in the face of unsurmountable tragedy left me awestruck. They became the characters." — Karan Johar

He called the series "devastating and brilliant in equal measure," and added that he "may not recover soon" from it. When the industry's most quotable man is this rattled, you pay attention.


**Raakh** — the word means ash — is built on the bones of a true horror. The series fictionalises the infamous 1978 Ranga-Billa case, in which siblings Geeta and Sanjay Chopra were abducted and murdered in Delhi, a crime so brutal it shook the nation and ended in the 1982 execution of both kidnappers. Here the children become Suman and Sahil Arora, and the case becomes the obsession of **Ali Fazal**'s SI Jayprakash Jatav, a young officer fighting both a killer and the prejudice of his own caste.

Fazal is in superb form. Critics single out the "aching sincerity" he brings to a dismissed rookie who stakes everything on a case nobody wants him to solve. But the real conversation is about craft. Director **Prosit Roy** — reuniting with Prime Video after the cult favourite *Paatal Lok* — and cinematographer Saumyananda Sahi keep you in a state of near-constant dread. The Hollywood Reporter India called the first two episodes "suffocating, immersive and terrifying," a crime drama packaged as a horror story.

It is not flawless. The same review notes that across eight episodes the longform demands creep in — subplots multiply, cold opens pile up, and the show hands nearly half its runtime to the killers Babu (a chaotic, Jekyll-and-Hyde **Akash Makhija**) and Rajjo (**Ramandeep Yadav**). There is a real question buried in there about whether a series can become more enamoured of its monsters than its victims. Some viewers will find it overlong. Almost none will find it forgettable.

For the diaspora, the math is simple. **Raakh** is streaming exclusively on **Amazon Prime Video** in Hindi, with subtitles, across more than 240 countries and territories — which means it landed in living rooms in New Jersey, Toronto and Wembley the same minute it did in Mumbai. No region-locking, no waiting for a delayed international window. If you have a Prime subscription, it is already sitting in your watchlist whether you put it there or not.

Created and co-directed by **Anusha Nandakumar** and **Sandeep Saket** and produced by Endemol Shine India, the series is meticulously researched and morally unwilling to offer easy answers — which is exactly why it is the conversation piece of the month. This is not weekend comfort viewing. It is the kind of show you watch in one tense, sleepless sitting and then sit in the dark thinking about.

Bendre once said she would return to acting only when the right role found her. It found her. The ash, it turns out, was worth the fire.
